column2: So he spoke, and they all became hushed in silence,
held by enchantment through the shadowy halls.
And Alcinous answered him again and spoke:

O Odysseus, since you have come to my bronze-floored,
5	high-roofed house, I think you will not, driven back again,
6	wander from your return, even though you have suffered very much.
7	And to each man of you I say this, charging you,
8	as many as in my halls always drink the elders' gleaming wine
9	and listen to the singer.
10	Clothes already lie for the guest in a well-polished chest
11	and intricately wrought gold and all the other
12	gifts, as many as the Phaeacians' counsellors brought here;
13	but come, let us give him a great tripod and a cauldron,
14	each man; and we in turn, collecting through the people,
15	shall repay ourselves; for it is hard for one man to give freely.
So spoke Alcinous, and his word pleased them.
They went each to his house to lie down;
and when early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
they hurried to the ship, and carried the man-honouring bronze.
And the sacred might of Alcinous stowed it well,
going himself through the ship beneath the benches, lest it
hinder any of the comrades as they rowed, when they strained at the oars.
And they went to Alcinous's house and prepared the feast.
And for them the sacred might of Alcinous sacrificed an ox
to Zeus of the dark clouds, son of Kronos, who rules over all.
And burning the thighs they feasted on the glorious feast
with delight; and among them the divine singer sang,
Demodocus, honoured by the people. But Odysseus
kept turning his head towards the all-shining sun,
eager for it to set; for he longed to go.
As when a man longs for supper, whose two wine-dark oxen
all day through the fallow field have dragged the jointed plough;
gladly for him the light of the sun goes down,
to go to supper, and his knees fail him as he goes;
so gladly for Odysseus the light of the sun went down.
And at once he spoke among the Phaeacians, lovers of oars,
and to Alcinous especially he addressed his word:

Lord Alcinous, most distinguished of all people,
39	send me off, having poured libations, unharmed; and you yourselves, farewell.
40	For already is accomplished what my dear heart wished,
41	a sending and dear gifts, which may the gods of heaven
42	make blessed for me; and may I find at home my blameless wife,
43	returned, with my dear ones safe.
44	And you, staying here, may you gladden your wedded wives
45	and children; and may the gods grant every kind
46	of excellence, and may no evil come upon the people.
So he spoke, and they all approved and bade
send off the guest, since he had spoken as was right.
And then the sacred might of Alcinous spoke to the herald:

Pontonous, mix a bowl and serve wine
51	to all in the hall, so that having prayed to father Zeus
52	we may send the guest to his own fatherland.
So he said, and Pontonous mixed honey-sweet wine,
and served all, standing by each; and they poured
libations to the blessed gods who hold the broad heaven,
right there from their seats. And divine Odysseus stood up,
and put in Arete's hand the two-handled cup,
and spoke to her winged words:

Farewell to me, O queen, continually, until old age
60	comes, and death, which befall men.
61	But I go; and you, be glad in this house
62	in your children and people and king Alcinous.
So saying, divine Odysseus stepped over the threshold,
and with him the sacred might of Alcinous sent a herald
to lead to the swift ship and the sea-shore;
and Arete sent women servants with him,
one carrying a well-washed robe and a tunic,
and another she gave him to carry a stout chest;
and another carried food and red wine.
And when they had come down to the ship and the sea,
at once the noble escorts took these things
and put them in the hollow ship, all the drink and food;
and for Odysseus they spread a rug and a linen sheet
on the deck of the hollow ship, at the stern, so that he might sleep undisturbed;
and he himself went aboard and lay down
in silence; and they sat each at the oars
in order, and loosed the cable from the pierced stone.
As soon as they leaned back and tossed the brine with the oar-blade,
sweet sleep fell on his eyelids,
unwaking, most sweet, most like to death.
And she, as on a plain four stallions yoked together,
all starting at once under the blows of the whip,
rising high, swiftly accomplish their course,
so her stern rose up, and behind it the great dark
wave of the loud-roaring sea surged.
And she ran very safely, steadily; and not even a hawk,
a falcon, the lightest of winged things, could keep up.
So she, running swiftly, cut the waves of the sea,
carrying a man with counsels like those of the gods,
who before had suffered very many pains in his heart,
passing through wars of men and grievous waves,
but now slept quietly, forgetting all he had suffered.
When the brightest star rose, which most of all
comes announcing the light of early-born Dawn,
at that time the sea-going ship drew near the island.
There is a harbour of Phorcys, the old man of the sea,
in the land of Ithaca; and two projecting headlands in it,
sheer, sloping down to the harbour,
which shelter from the great wave of the stormy winds
outside; and inside without moorings stay
well-benched ships, when they reach the mooring place.
And at the head of the harbour is a long-leaved olive,
and near it a lovely misty cave,
sacred to the nymphs who are called Naiads.
And in it are bowls and two-handled jars
of stone; and there bees store their honey.
And in it are very long looms of stone, where the nymphs
weave sea-purple webs, a wonder to see;
and in it ever-flowing water. And it has two doors,
one towards the North Wind, by which men go down,
and the other towards the South is more divine; and by that
men do not enter, but it is the way of the immortals.
Here they rowed in, knowing the place before; and the ship then
ran onto the land, up to half her length,
driven on; for such was the speed the hands of the rowers gave her.
And they, stepping from the well-benched ship onto the land,
first lifted Odysseus out of the hollow ship
with his linen and shining rug,
and laid him on the sand, bound in sleep,
and took out the goods, which the noble Phaeacians
had given him as he went home, through great-hearted Athena.
And these they put together at the foot of the olive
off the road, lest some passing man,
before Odysseus woke, come and harm them;
and they themselves went back home again. And the Earth-shaker
did not forget the threats which he had first
threatened against godlike Odysseus, and he asked Zeus's purpose:

Father Zeus, I shall no longer be honoured among the immortal gods,
129	when mortals do not honour me at all,
130	the Phaeacians, who are indeed of my own stock.
131	For even now I said that Odysseus, after suffering many evils,
132	would come home; but his return I never took away
133	altogether, since you first promised and nodded assent.
134	But they, bringing him asleep in a swift ship over the sea,
135	have set him down in Ithaca, and given him countless gifts,
136	bronze and gold in plenty and woven clothing,
137	much, as Odysseus would never have won from Troy,
138	even if he had come unharmed, having received his share of the spoil.
And answering him cloud-gathering Zeus said:

Alas, Earth-shaker of wide strength, what have you said.
141	The gods do not dishonour you; and it would be hard
142	to cast dishonours on the oldest and best.
143	But if any of men, yielding to force and strength,
144	does not honour you, you have vengeance always hereafter.
145	Do as you wish and as is dear to your heart.
And then Poseidon the Earth-shaker answered him:

At once I would do, dark-clouded one, as you say;
148	but I always respect and avoid your heart.
149	Now I wish to smash the very beautiful ship of the Phaeacians,
150	as it comes back from the sending, on the misty sea,
151	so that they may now stop, and cease from escorting
152	men, and to cover their city with a great mountain.
And answering him cloud-gathering Zeus said:

My friend, as it seems best to my heart,
155	when all the people look out from the city
156	and see her driven in, make a stone near the land
157	like a swift ship, so that all
158	men may wonder, and cover their city with a great mountain.
But when Poseidon the Earth-shaker heard this,
he went to Scheria, where the Phaeacians were born.
There he waited; and the sea-going ship came very near,
swiftly driven; and near her came the Earth-shaker,
who turned her to stone and rooted her below,
striking with his hand pressed down; and he went away.
And they spoke winged words to one another,
the Phaeacians of long oars, men famed for ships.
And so one would say, looking at his neighbour:

Alas, who has bound the swift ship in the sea
169	as she was driven home? And now she was in full view.
So one would say; but they did not know how it had come about.
And among them Alcinous spoke and said:

Alas, indeed the old oracles of my father reach me now,
173	who said that Poseidon was angry
174	with us, because we are unharmed escorts of all.
175	He said that one day a very beautiful ship of Phaeacian men,
176	coming back from an escort, on the misty sea
177	he would smash, and cover our city with a great mountain.
178	So the old man said; and now all this is being fulfilled.
179	But come, as I say, let us all obey:
180	cease from escorting mortals, whenever anyone comes
181	to our city; and to Poseidon let us sacrifice
182	twelve chosen bulls, in case he pities us,
183	and does not cover our city with a very long mountain.
So he spoke, and they were afraid, and prepared the bulls.
So they prayed to lord Poseidon,
the leaders and rulers of the Phaeacian people,
standing around the altar. And divine Odysseus woke
asleep in his fatherland, and did not know it,
having been long away; for around him the goddess had poured a mist,
Pallas Athena, daughter of Zeus, so that she might make him
unrecognizable and tell him each thing,
lest his wife or townsmen or friends know him
before the suitors had paid for all their outrage.
Therefore everything looked strange to the lord,
the long paths and the safe harbours
and the sheer rocks and the flourishing trees.
He stood up, springing, and looked at his fatherland;
and he groaned, and struck both his thighs
with his hands pressed down, and lamenting he spoke a word:

Woe is me, to the land of what mortals have I come again?
201	Are they insolent and savage and unjust,
202	or hospitable, and is their mind god-fearing?
203	Where am I carrying all this wealth? Where do I myself
204	wander? Would that I had stayed with the Phaeacians
205	there; and I would have gone to some other of the mighty kings,
206	who would have befriended me and sent me on my way.
207	Now I know neither where to put it, nor will I
208	leave it here, lest it become spoil for others.
209	Alas, so they were not wholly wise nor just,
210	the leaders and rulers of the Phaeacians,
211	who brought me to another land, and said indeed
212	that they would take me to clear-seen Ithaca, but did not fulfil it.
213	May Zeus, protector of suppliants, punish them, who oversees other
214	men too and punishes whoever does wrong.
215	But come, let me count the goods and see,
216	lest they have gone off, taking something in the hollow ship.
So saying he counted the very beautiful tripods and cauldrons
and the gold and the fair woven garments.
Of these nothing was lacking; but he mourned for his fatherland
creeping along the shore of the loud-roaring sea,
lamenting much. And near him came Athena,
like a young man in form, a shepherd of flocks,
very delicate, such as the sons of lords are,
with a well-made double cloak about her shoulders;
and under her smooth feet she had sandals, and in her hands a javelin.
Odysseus was glad at the sight of her and went to meet her,
and spoke to her winged words:

Friend, since you are the first I meet in this place,
229	hail, and may you not meet me with evil mind,
230	but save these things, and save me; for to you
231	I pray as to a god, and come to your dear knees.
232	And tell me this truly, that I may know well:
233	what land, what people, what men are born here?
234	Is it some clear-seen island, or a shore
235	of the rich-soiled mainland leaning on the sea?
And the goddess grey-eyed Athena answered him:

You are a fool, stranger, or have come from far away,
238	if you ask about this land. It is not so very
239	nameless; very many know it,
240	both those who live toward the dawn and the sun,
241	and those who live behind towards the misty gloom.
242	It is indeed rugged and not fit for driving horses,
243	nor very poor, though not made wide.
244	For in it is boundless grain, and in it wine
245	is made; and rain always holds it and flourishing dew;
246	and it is good for goats and cattle; there is wood
247	of every kind, and watering-places throughout the year.
248	Therefore, stranger, the name of Ithaca has reached even to Troy,
249	which they say is far from the Achaean land.
So she spoke, and much-enduring divine Odysseus was glad,
rejoicing in his fatherland, as Pallas Athena
daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus told him;
and he spoke to her winged words:
yet he did not speak truly, but took back his word,
always turning in his breast a mind of many wiles:

I heard of Ithaca even in broad Crete,
257	far over the sea; and now I have come myself
258	with these goods; and leaving as much more to my children
259	I flee, since I killed the dear son of Idomeneus,
260	Orsilochus, swift of foot, who in broad Crete
261	surpassed bread-eating men with his swift feet,
262	because he wished to deprive me of all the Trojan
263	spoil, for the sake of which I suffered pains in my heart,
264	passing through wars of men and grievous waves,
265	because I did not serve his father to gratify him
266	in the land of the Trojans, but led other comrades.
267	Him I struck with a bronze-tipped spear as he came back
268	from the field, lying in ambush by the road with a comrade;
269	and a very dark night held the sky, nor did any
270	man notice us, and I escaped notice in taking his life.
271	But when I had killed him with the sharp bronze,
272	at once I went to a ship and begged the noble Phoenicians,
273	and gave them spoil to their heart's content;
274	I bade them land me at Pylos and set me ashore,
275	or in divine Elis, where the Epeians rule.
276	But the force of the wind drove them away from there,
277	much against their will, and they did not wish to deceive me.
278	Driven off from there we came here by night.
279	We rowed hastily into the harbour, and none of us
280	thought of supper, though we greatly needed to take it,
281	but just as we were we disembarked and all lay down.
282	There sweet sleep came upon me, exhausted,
283	and they took my goods out of the hollow ship
284	and put them down where I myself lay on the sand.
285	And they, going up to well-inhabited Sidon,
286	went away; but I was left behind, grieved at heart.
So he spoke, and the goddess grey-eyed Athena smiled,
and stroked him with her hand; and she took the form of a woman
fair and tall and skilled in splendid works;
and she spoke to him winged words:

He would be crafty and a cheat who could outdo you
292	in all manner of wiles, even if a god should meet you.
293	Hardy man, of many wiles, insatiate of tricks, so you were not to
294	cease, even in your own land, from deceits
295	and thievish tales, which are dear to you from the ground up.
296	But come, let us speak of this no longer, both knowing
297	cunning, since you are far the best of all mortals
298	in counsel and speech, and I among all the gods
299	am famed for wit and cunning; and yet you did not know
300	Pallas Athena, daughter of Zeus, who always
301	stand by you in all your labours and guard you,
302	and made you dear to all the Phaeacians,
303	and now again I have come here, to weave a plan with you
304	and to hide the goods, as many as the noble Phaeacians
305	gave you as you went home, by my counsel and mind,
306	and to tell how much fate has for you in your well-built house
307	of troubles to endure; and you must bear them even under compulsion,
308	and not tell anyone, neither man nor woman,
309	of all, that you have come back wandering, but in silence
310	suffer many pains, submitting to the violence of men.
And answering her wise Odysseus said:

It is hard, goddess, for a mortal who meets you to know you,
313	even a very knowing one; for you liken yourself to anyone.
314	But this I know well, that you were kind to me before,
315	while we sons of the Achaeans fought in Troy.
316	But when we had sacked the steep city of Priam,
317	and went in our ships, and a god scattered the Achaeans,
318	I did not afterwards see you, daughter of Zeus, nor notice you
319	come aboard my ship, to ward off some pain from me.
320	But always keeping my heart torn within my breast
321	I wandered, until the gods freed me from my misery;
322	until, in the rich land of the Phaeacian men,
323	you encouraged me with words and yourself led me to the city.
324	Now I beseech you by your father—for I do not think
325	that I have come to clear-seen Ithaca, but that I am turning about
326	in some other land; and I think you are mocking me
327	in saying this, to deceive my wits—
328	tell me whether I truly have come to my dear fatherland.
And then the goddess grey-eyed Athena answered him:

Always you have such a thought in your breast;
331	therefore I cannot leave you, unhappy as you are,
332	because you are well-spoken and quick-witted and prudent.
333	For gladly another man, coming back from wandering,
334	would be eager to see his children and wife in his halls;
335	but to you it is not yet dear to learn or to ask,
336	until you first test your wife, who just
337	sits in the halls, and wretched for her always
338	the nights and days wear away as she sheds tears.
339	But I never doubted, but in my heart
340	knew that you would return, having lost all your comrades;
341	but I did not wish to fight with Poseidon,
342	my father's brother, who laid up wrath in his heart against you,
343	angry that you blinded his dear son.
344	But come, I shall show you the seat of Ithaca, that you may be assured.
345	This is the harbour of Phorcys, the old man of the sea,
346	and this at the head of the harbour is the long-leaved olive;
347	and near it the lovely misty cave,
348	sacred to the nymphs who are called Naiads;
349	and this is the vaulted cave, where you
350	used to offer the nymphs many perfect hecatombs;
351	and this is Mount Neriton clothed in forest.
So saying the goddess scattered the mist, and the land appeared;
and much-enduring divine Odysseus was glad,
rejoicing in his land, and kissed the grain-giving earth.
And at once he prayed to the nymphs, lifting up his hands:

Nymphs, Naiads, daughters of Zeus, I never thought
357	I should see you again; now rejoice in my gentle prayers;
358	and we shall give gifts too, as before,
359	if the daughter of Zeus, the driver of spoil, willingly lets me
360	live myself and makes my dear son grow.
And again the goddess grey-eyed Athena spoke to him:

Take heart, let not these things trouble your mind.
363	But let us put the goods in the recess of the marvellous cave
364	at once now, so that they remain safe for you;
365	and let us ourselves consider how it may be best.
So saying the goddess entered the misty cave,
searching out hiding-places in the cave; and Odysseus
brought everything nearer, gold and unwearying bronze
and well-made clothes, which the Phaeacians had given him.
And these he laid away well, and a stone she set on the door,
Pallas Athena, daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus.
And the two, sitting down by the root of the sacred olive,
planned destruction for the overbearing suitors.
And among them the goddess grey-eyed Athena began to speak:

Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of many devices,
376	consider how you will lay hands on the shameless suitors,
377	who for three years now lord it through your hall,
378	wooing your godlike wife and offering bridal gifts;
379	and she, always lamenting your return in her heart,
380	gives hope to all and makes promises to each man,
381	sending messages, but her mind purposes otherwise.
And answering her wise Odysseus said:

Alas, I was indeed about to perish by the evil fate of
384	Agamemnon son of Atreus in my halls,
385	if you, goddess, had not told me each thing in due order.
386	But come, weave a plan, how I may pay them back;
387	and stand by me yourself, putting in me daring courage,
388	such as when we loosed Troy's shining veils.
389	If you would stand by me so eagerly, grey-eyed one,
390	I would even fight with three hundred men
391	with you, lady goddess, if you helped me readily.
And then the goddess grey-eyed Athena answered him:

Indeed I shall be with you, and you will not escape my notice,
394	when we get on with these things; and I think some
395	of the suitors, who devour your livelihood, will spatter
396	the boundless floor with blood and brains.
397	But come, I shall make you unrecognizable to all mortals;
398	I shall wither the fair skin on your supple limbs,
399	and destroy the yellow hair from your head, and put about you
400	a rag that one would loathe to see on a man,
401	and I shall dim your eyes, which before were very beautiful,
402	so that you may appear squalid to all the suitors
403	and to your wife and the son whom you left in your halls.
404	And you yourself first go to the swineherd,
405	who is the keeper of your pigs, and is likewise kindly to you,
406	and loves your son and prudent Penelope.
407	You will find him sitting by the swine; and they feed
408	by the rock of the Raven and the spring of Arethusa,
409	eating acorns to their heart's content and drinking
410	the black water, which makes swine grow flourishing fat.
411	Stay there, and sitting by him ask about everything,
412	until I come to Sparta of fair women,
413	to call Telemachus, your dear son, Odysseus;
414	who went to wide Lacedaemon, to Menelaus,
415	to inquire after news of you, if anywhere you were still alive.
And answering her wise Odysseus said:

Why then did you not tell him, knowing all in your mind?
418	Is it that he too may suffer pains wandering
419	on the barren sea, while others devour his livelihood?
And then the goddess grey-eyed Athena answered him:

Let him not be too much on your mind.
422	I myself escorted him, that he might win good renown
423	by going there; but he has no toil, but at ease
424	sits in the house of the son of Atreus, and boundless stores lie by him.
425	Indeed young men lie in wait for him with a black ship,
426	eager to kill him, before he reaches his fatherland;
427	but I think not, before the earth holds some
428	of the suitors, who devour your livelihood.
So saying, Athena touched him with her wand.
She withered the fair skin on his supple limbs,
and destroyed the yellow hair from his head, and around his
whole limbs put the skin of an old man,
and dimmed his eyes, which before were very beautiful;
and about him she threw another foul rag and a tunic,
tattered and filthy, stained with evil smoke;
and about him she put the great hide of a swift stag,
bald; and she gave him a staff and a mean wallet,
full of holes; and in it was a twisted rope for a strap.
These two, having so planned, parted. And she then
went to divine Lacedaemon to the son of Odysseus.
